title: Schemas & search_path Resolution
description: Organize database objects into schemas, configure search_path resolution, and implement multi-tenant schema isolation.

data.text: A **schema** in PostgreSQL is a namespace within a database that contains tables, views, functions, and types. By default, all objects are created in the `public` schema. Using custom schemas is common for modular architecture and multi-tenant SaaS applications.
When you execute `SELECT * FROM users`, PostgreSQL searches schemas in the order defined by the **`search_path`** parameter (analogous to the `PATH` environment variable in Linux).

data.title: Configuring search_path for Tenant Isolation
data.content: Switching schemas dynamically based on tenant.

data.text: Why Use Schemas Instead of Many Databases?
Schemas let you separate concerns while keeping everything joinable in one transaction. The two patterns you will meet in real systems are:

items: **Modular monolith** — one schema per bounded context (`billing`, `inventory`, `auth`) with clear ownership. `SELECT ... FROM billing.invoices JOIN auth.users ...` still works.
**Schema-per-tenant** — every tenant gets `tenant_acme`, `tenant_globex`, … with identical table shapes. Strong isolation, but migrations must iterate over every schema.

data.text: An unqualified name such as `invoices` is looked up in each schema on `search_path`, left to right; the first match wins. Only the first schema is used for `CREATE`, which means a misconfigured path can silently create tables in an unexpected place.

data.title: The `search_path` Privilege Trap
data.text: If an application sets `search_path = public` and a low-privileged role can create objects in `public`, that role can shadow real tables or functions. Remove `CREATE` on `public` from untrusted roles (`REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;`) and always schema-qualify security-definer functions.

data.title: Listing Schemas, Owners, and Object Counts
data.content: Useful when auditing a database with many schemas.
data.code:
SELECT n.nspname AS schema,
       pg_get_userbyid(n.nspowner) AS owner,
       count(c.oid) FILTER (WHERE c.relkind = 'r') AS tables,
       count(c.oid) FILTER (WHERE c.relkind = 'v') AS views
FROM pg_namespace n
LEFT JOIN pg_class c ON c.relnamespace = n.oid
WHERE n.nspname NOT LIKE 'pg_%' AND n.nspname <> 'information_schema'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 3 DESC;

-- Move a table between schemas
ALTER TABLE public.legacy_orders SET SCHEMA archive;

-- DROP SCHEMA refuses if it contains objects; CASCADE removes them all
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS tenant_deleted CASCADE;

items.question: What is the difference between a database and a schema?
items.answer: A database is an isolated catalog that a connection is bound to; a schema is a namespace within a database. You can join across schemas in one query, but not across databases.

items.question: What does `search_path` do?
items.answer: It lists the schemas consulted, in order, to resolve unqualified object names. The first schema is also where new objects are created.

items.question: What happens if two schemas on `search_path` contain a table with the same name?
items.answer: The earlier schema wins. Qualify the name to avoid ambiguity, and remember only the first schema is used for `CREATE TABLE`.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A schema is a namespace inside one database: objects in different schemas are still joinable.
`search_path` resolves unqualified names left-to-right and determines where new objects are created.
`USAGE` controls visibility, `CREATE` controls whether a role can add objects — grant them separately.
Harden `public`: untrusted roles should not have `CREATE` on it, and security-definer functions should set an explicit `search_path`.
data.takeaway: Mention `search_path` security when you are asked about schemas — it shows production awareness, not just syntax.
